    Reference · read this once, properly

    Not financial advice

    The full disclaimer: what Bablytics is, what its output is and is not, the particular risks of options, the exact policy on money, and why nothing here is a recommendation.

    Bablytics is a research and entertainment tool. Nothing it produces is a recommendation to buy or sell anything. Grades, memos, leans, levels, projections and predictions are model output — frequently wrong, never personalised, and not reviewed by any licensed professional. The software does not trade on its own; the only way an order reaches a broker is your own explicit click on one order at a time, after you have chosen to connect a brokerage. The UI carries this disclaimer permanently, the README carries it, and so does every page of this Guide.

    What Bablytics is#

    A personal research tool, built by its owner to study his own account and his own decisions. It runs on your computer, keeps its record in a folder you own, and is offered as software — not as a service, not as a newsletter, not as a signal feed. There is no subscription, no account with anyone, and nobody on the other end. If you run it, you are running a program, and what you do with its output is entirely yours.

    Its subject is the market’s infinite library of noise (the name): the point of the board is to argue, score itself against the tape, and keep an honest record of being wrong. That record — the Evening Court, the Pyramid, the dossiers, the League, the Model Card — exists so the output can be judged, not so it can be trusted.

    What the output is — and is not#

    • It is model output. In real mode the board members are a large language model wearing persona prompts; in mock mode they are deterministic heuristics. Either way a grade is a number a program produced from public data and its own prior record. It is not the opinion of a person, and the personas are not people.
    • It is frequently wrong. The app measures this and shows you: calibration per member, hit rates, the Pyramid, realized 1-day and 5-day outcomes on every lead, the court’s own grade-versus-outcome correlation. Read those numbers as what they are — evidence about a model, on a small sample, in one stretch of one market.
    • It is never personalised. The board does not know your finances, your obligations, your time horizon, your tax position or your tolerance for loss. The Pulse’s “goals” are two words you pick from two short lists; they shape a bracket of arithmetic, they are not a suitability assessment, and nothing in the app is one.
    • It is not reviewed by anyone licensed. No investment adviser, broker-dealer, or other regulated person checks, approves or stands behind anything the software writes.
    • It is not an offer or a solicitation. A lead with a selected option contract is a research label — “this is the expression the board discussed” — not an invitation to buy that contract.

    Options carry particular risk#

    Half of every morning’s leads are option contracts, because that is what the flow scan surfaces. Options are leveraged, time-limited instruments: a bought call or put can lose its entire premium, and often does; spreads and short options can lose more than was paid or collected; time decay works against a holder every day; assignment and exercise have mechanics of their own; and the prices the app shows come from a delayed public chain, not an executable quote. One of the board’s own seats is built around “expect every option to go to zero” for a reason. If you do not already understand the risk disclosures your own broker required you to read before trading options, this software is not the place to learn them.

    No fiduciary, no adviser, no duty of care#

    Neither the software nor its author is your investment adviser, broker, fiduciary or agent, and using Bablytics creates no such relationship. The author is not a registered investment adviser or broker-dealer and is not offering advice to you or anyone. Nothing here accounts for your circumstances, and no output is a promise of any result. If you want advice, talk to someone who is licensed to give it and who knows your situation; bring the app’s output along as a conversation piece if you like, but not as a plan.

    The exact policy on money#

    Stated precisely, because vagueness here would be a kind of lie:

    • The morning pipeline, the Pre-Open Check, the Midday Check-In, the Evening Court, the horizon reviews, the Pulse, the Bailiff and the Paper League have no execution path. Those modules cannot construct, route or transmit an order; the Pulse and Bailiff packages never import the broker code or touch the order table. The Bailiff “closes legs” in the board’s own record and the paper ledger — never a real position. Every Pulse payload is stamped “Model opinion — not financial advice; nothing executes.” and every Bailiff surface “The Bailiff closes legs in the record only — never the broker, never your money.”
    • The Broker view is the one place the app can touch a real account, and only after you create a Schwab developer app, enter its key and secret, and complete Schwab’s OAuth flow. Until then a submit returns “Connect Schwab in Settings”.
    • Once connected, the bot stages orders from the morning leads into a queue you can edit or cancel. A real-money order is never submitted without an explicit click in the UI — one order per click, each behind a confirmation that restates ticker, side, quantity and price. There is no “submit all”, no server-side loop over orders, no standing auto-submit setting anywhere, and the only code path that reaches the broker’s order endpoint is the one behind that single click.
    • The moment you click Submit, the trade is yours: your account, your decision, your risk, your responsibility — exactly as if you had typed it into your broker’s own screen.

    Paper results are not money#

    The League’s equity curves, the Bot’s record, the outcome model’s metrics, the Pulse population’s held-out rewards and the Model Card’s tables are simulations and evaluations on historical or paper data. They ignore slippage, fills, borrow, commissions, taxes and the fact that a real order moves the price. They are published so the machinery can be judged; they are not a track record, and they are certainly not a forecast of what any of it would do with real money.

    The data may be late, incomplete or wrong#

    Quotes, option chains, headlines, economic releases and congressional disclosures come from free public sources (listed here) with their own delays, gaps and errors. Collectors are written to degrade rather than crash, which means a session can run on partial data and say so in a note you might not read. Treat every number as a claim to verify against your broker before acting on anything.

    About the personas#

    Several seats are written after the public philosophies of real people — Sam Parikh (SmarterTrading411), Warren Buffett, Benjamin Graham and Nassim Taleb — and one after the owner’s own paper, Hedging the Wheel. They paraphrase published ideas for personal research. They are not those people, do not speak for them, and nothing here is endorsed by them. The Borges of the product’s name is a story, not a spokesman.

    Your own account, your own call#

    The owner built this to hold himself to account: the TAKE toggle, the mandatory reflections after a loss, the scorecard the weekend review reads back to him. If you run it, you inherit that posture and not a guarantee. You are responsible for every decision you make with or without this software; you accept the risk of loss, including the loss of everything you put at risk; and you agree that the author and contributors are not liable for any outcome. The software is provided as is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied.

    Where this disclaimer lives in the product#

    • The footer of every view in the app: Research tool — not financial advice. Grades are model output, not recommendations.
    • The Disclaimer panel on the Settings view, and the README of the repository.
    • The Pulse and Bailiff disclaimer strings, stamped on their API payloads and every screen that renders them.
    • The PDF exports and this Guide — on the strip at the foot of every page.

    If any of this is unwelcome, the honest response is the right one: do not use the output to make decisions about money.
